attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Accurately captures the near-annual promises since 2014, the beta status, and the need for constant supervision. The closing robotaxi line ('likely') is a separate, hedged sentence and is correctly left out.

contract.note: A fair, ordinary reading: roughly annual predictions without identical deadlines, and 'driverless' meaning no continuous supervision. Using September 2022 software documentation fits the post's date.

evidence.note: 2014 Nikkei prediction of full autopilot within five or six years. It is hedged ('probably') but is still a public autonomy prediction.
Dated chronology with autonomy predictions in 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019.
July 2020 prediction of level-five autonomy by year end. It also notes the then-current system needed an alert driver.
January 2022 prediction of full self-driving that year. The 2021 prediction is cited, but that part of the article is not in the excerpt.
Tesla's Q2 2022 disclosure calls the program FSD Beta and 'supervised'. It is a company disclosure, which is appropriate for the software's status.
September 2022 FSD Beta instructions require attention at all times, and TechCrunch corroborates the release timing.

reviews.rationale: Dated records show autonomy predictions in almost every year from 2014 to 2022. Tesla's own materials from mid and late 2022 describe FSD as a beta that requires continuous driver attention. The evidence contains no sign of unsupervised operation before the post. Both components hold.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: Narrowing to 'technology projects' is a reasonable reading in context. It is a firm general characterization with no quantified threshold.

contract.note: The plain reading (on-time delivery as the exception, across a representative set of deadlines) is ordinary and fair. Because 'almost never' has no numeric meaning and the set of deadlines is undefined, the result depends on how the inventory is built.

evidence.note: One documented miss (robotaxis by 2020). A single instance cannot establish a frequency.
Tesla's self-reported early Model Y deliveries. This is a company claim about its own schedule, and one exception does not refute 'almost never'.

reviews.rationale: The packet has one miss and one claimed early delivery. It has no representative list of deadlines due by September 2022, so the rate of on-time delivery cannot be measured. The stated gaps confirm this. The evidence does not settle 'almost never'.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'apparently' qualifier. It drops the uncontested October 2019 demo element but is otherwise faithful.

contract.note: 'Apparently' shows Marcus was relaying the 2021 reports of the shutdown. Requiring the shutdown itself to fall in calendar 2021, rather than its reporting, is stricter than his hedged wording warrants, and the date result depends on that reading.

evidence.note: October 2019 OpenAI paper on solving a Rubik's cube with a robot hand, which confirms the demo.
July 2021 confirmation that the robotics team was disbanded 'as of recently'. This supports a shutdown but leaves its exact date open.
A 2025 retrospective that dates the shutdown to October 2020, without giving its source. It conflicts with e2's 'recently' and so does not settle the date.

reviews.rationale: The demo is confirmed and a shutdown did occur. The date is contested: e3 says October 2020, while e2 says 'recently' as of July 2021. The packet also states that the absence of any shipped product was not independently established. With a contested date and an unverified product component, the evidence does not settle the claim.
